title: loadManifest swallows fs error cause; original errno (EACCES, EISDIR) is lost
description: The try/catch around fs.readFile rethrows a fixed string ('Deployment manifest not found at <path>...') for ANY readFile failure — ENOENT (the only case the user-visible message claims), EACCES (permission), EISDIR (path is a directory), EMFILE, etc. The original error is dropped on the floor: no `cause`, no error code, no log. A user whose manifest exists but is unreadable due to perms will see a misleading 'not found' message and chase the wrong fix.
impact: Misleading error UI for non-ENOENT failures. Operator wastes time re-running `pnpm deploy-all` (which won't fix a permissions issue) instead of seeing the real errno. Diagnostic info is permanently lost — there is no console.error fallback either.
recommendation: Either (a) discriminate on `(err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code` and only claim 'not found' when code === 'ENOENT', falling through to a generic 'manifest unreadable: <code>' message for other cases, or (b) attach `{ cause: err }` to the rethrown Error so downstream consumers can introspect.

title: JSON.parse on manifest is unguarded; malformed JSON throws raw SyntaxError
description:
After fs.readFile succeeds, `JSON.parse(raw)` is called with no try/catch. If the manifest file exists but contains invalid JSON (truncated write from `pnpm deploy-all` mid-flight, accidental editor save, BOM, etc.), the loader throws a bare `SyntaxError: Unexpected token ... in JSON at position N` with no manifest path, no bootstrap hint, and no indication this is a manifest-shape problem. The App component will surface this verbatim in 
{state.error}
without any actionable context.
impact: User sees a confusing JS-internals error instead of the actionable inline error required by AC1.1 / AC1.2 ('actionable error pointing at the bootstrap recipe'). Mid-deploy race with the sandbox's manifest write is plausible — the contract explicitly mentions sandbox restart as a real condition.
recommendation: Wrap JSON.parse in try/catch and rethrow with the same actionable shape used for ENOENT: `Deployment manifest at ${manifestPath} is not valid JSON: <inner.message>. ${BOOTSTRAP_HINT}`.

title: Manifest loader does not validate per-pool entry shape; missing fields silently become undefined
description: loadManifest validates that `parsed.pools` is an object and that `packages.deepbook.packageId` is a non-empty string, but does NOT validate that each entry under `pools` has the three load-bearing fields (`poolId`, `baseCoinType`, `quoteCoinType`). The `Object.entries(parsed.pools).map(...)` blindly trusts each entry; if a sandbox manifest is partially written or the schema drifts (e.g. a future sandbox renames `poolId` to `pool_id`), the loader returns `PoolDescriptor` records with `poolId: undefined` cast as a string. Downstream `sui_getObject` will then be called with `undefined` as the object id, producing a cryptic RPC error far from the root cause.
impact: Schema drift in the sandbox manifest produces silent data corruption rather than the clear validation error AC1.2 is meant to guarantee. T-004 covers the missing-`pools`-key case but no test covers a malformed pool entry; this is a blind spot for the same dimension AC1.2 asks the loader to defend.
recommendation: After Object.entries, validate that each entry's `poolId`, `baseCoinType`, and `quoteCoinType` are non-empty strings; throw a specific 'Manifest pool <symbol> is missing field <name>' error otherwise. Mirror the check style already used for `packages.deepbook.packageId`.

title: main.tsx loadManifest path uses unguarded JSON.parse and no validation
description: The production runtime (browser path) does NOT use the validated `loadManifest` from `manifest.ts` — it inlines its own loader: fetch → text → JSON.parse → object access. The fetched body is JSON.parse'd with no try/catch (so a truncated/invalid manifest crashes with a raw SyntaxError surfaced into the React error message), the `packageId` is silently coerced via `?? ''` (so a missing package id produces an empty string instead of the actionable error the unit-tested loader would throw), and per-pool entries are NOT validated for required fields (same blind spot as R3-003 but in the path users actually hit). The unit-tested validations in `manifest.ts` are dead code at runtime — `void loadManifest;` on line 59 even confesses this.
impact: Every manifest-validation guarantee proven by T-003 / T-004 is bypassed in production. A missing `packages.deepbook.packageId` silently becomes `''` and surfaces as confusing downstream RPC failures (filter `MoveModule.package: ''`) instead of the inline 'Deployment manifest is missing packages.deepbook.packageId' error. The cycle's error-UX promise (AC1.1/AC1.2 actionable error) holds in tests but not in the deployed SPA.
recommendation: Refactor `loadManifest` to accept either a path (Node) or a fetched string (browser) — or extract a `parseManifest(raw, sourceLabel)` pure function that both code paths share. main.tsx should never re-implement the validation; current `void loadManifest;` is a tell that the dev knew this was wrong but didn't wire it up.

title: main.tsx fetchPoolStats stub silently returns empty data instead of throwing
description: The wired-up `fetchPoolStats` returns a hardcoded zero/undefined PoolCardData for every pool — no RPC call is made, no error is thrown. The user opens the app, sees N cards (one per pool, satisfying the visual layout) all showing '—' for every metric, and has no signal that the data layer is unimplemented. There is no console warning, no error UI, no degradation notice. This is a classic silent-failure pattern: the page renders, the user assumes the sandbox just has no activity, and the actual bug (no RPC integration wired) never surfaces.
impact: Silent data loss equivalent to a fully-stubbed app shipping as 'working'. A reviewer landing on the dev URL would see green cards with sentinel values and reasonably conclude the sandbox is idle, not that the data layer is missing. The error UI (AC1.1) is bypassed entirely because no error is thrown. This is the worst-class silent failure: a defective deliverable that looks healthy.
recommendation: Either (a) actually wire fetchPoolStats to runDataLayer / fetchFills / computeMarketStats / aggregateFills — these modules exist and are unit-tested but are not connected here — or (b) throw an explicit 'Slot 1 data layer is not yet wired (see RUNBOOK)' error so the inline error UI fires. Returning a structurally-valid but semantically empty result without warning violates the silent-failure-hunter rubric.
evidence:
fetchPoolStats: async (descriptor): Promise<PoolCardData> => ({
    poolId: descriptor.poolId,
    symbol: descriptor.symbol,
    volume24h: 0,
    lastPrice: undefined,
    midPrice: undefined,
    spread: undefined,
    depthWithinOnePercent: 0,
    sparkline: [],
  }),

title: main.tsx silently no-ops when #root element is missing
description: If `document.getElementById('root')` returns null (e.g. broken index.html, hot-reload race, mismatched id), the `if (root)` guard silently skips `createRoot(...).render(...)` and the page is left blank with no console error and no diagnostic. There is no else branch, no console.error, and no DOM message inserted to indicate the React tree never mounted.
impact: Blank page with zero diagnostic. AC1.1 requires the page to mount 'without console errors' for the success case but says nothing about silent-mount failure; this is technically AC-compliant but is a hostile UX: the dev or e2e reviewer hitting the URL gets nothing actionable. Low because index.html is correct today and the regression risk is small.
recommendation: Replace `if (root)` with a thrown error or `console.error('main.tsx: #root element missing in index.html')`. Silent skip is the wrong default for a fatal mounting precondition.

title: App.useEffect's Promise.all aborts at first failure; partial pool failures cause total error UI
description: App fetches per-pool stats with `Promise.all(manifest.pools.map(p => deps.fetchPoolStats(p)))`. If any single pool's fetchPoolStats rejects (e.g. one pool object is mid-upgrade, or one suix_queryEvents page errors), the entire batch rejects and the App switches to the global error UI. All other pools — which fetched successfully — are discarded. The user sees 'Could not load market data' even when N-1 of N pools are healthy. This violates the spirit of AC1.4/AC1.5 ('per-pool' rendering) by making one pool's transient failure poison the whole dashboard.
impact: Brittle error semantics. A single flaky pool blanks the entire dashboard. Sandbox restart races (the contract explicitly mentions this as plausible) will commonly knock out one pool's response while others are fine, producing an all-or-nothing error UI that obscures which pool is the problem.
recommendation: Use `Promise.allSettled` and render per-pool cards with a per-card error sentinel for failed pools (PoolCard already supports sentinel rendering via `fmt`). Reserve the page-level error UI for the manifest-load failure path, where the failure really is global.

title: App has no error boundary; render-time exception in PoolCard would blank-screen the page
description: App handles async load failures (the try/catch in useEffect) but provides no React error boundary around the rendered `<PoolCard>` list. If a PoolCard ever throws during render (e.g. a future addition to PoolCardData passes a non-finite sparkline value through a code path that bypasses `fmt`, or `data.sparkline.map` is called on a non-array because the data layer mis-shaped a response), React 19 will unmount the entire tree by default and show a blank page with only a console error. AC1.1 requires the page to render an actionable error; an unhandled render-time exception would break that contract silently.
impact: Edge-case render failures take down the whole app instead of degrading to the inline error UI. Today PoolCard is defensive (uses `fmt` sentinel) so practical risk is low, but the absence of an error boundary is a class-level gap in the error story.
recommendation: Wrap the PoolCard list (or App body) in a small ErrorBoundary class component that renders the same `<div role='alert'>` shell on render failure. This is a 20-line addition and closes the AC1.1 gap definitively.

title: rpc() does not check response.ok; non-2xx responses are JSON-parsed and may produce confusing errors
description: The `rpc` helper calls `fetch(...)` and immediately does `await response.json()` without checking `response.ok` or `response.status`. If the Sui RPC endpoint returns a 502/503 (gateway down), 404 (wrong path), or HTML error page (typical of a misconfigured proxy), `response.json()` will throw a SyntaxError ('Unexpected token < in JSON at position 0'). That error is then surfaced verbatim, with no indication that the underlying problem was an HTTP-level failure or unreachable endpoint — which is exactly the AC1.1 / T-020 scenario the inline error UI is supposed to handle gracefully.
impact: T-020 passes only because the test stubs `fetchPoolStats` to throw a pre-formatted message. Against a real unreachable RPC (network drop, sandbox down, wrong port), the user sees `SyntaxError: Unexpected token < ...` instead of the actionable RPC-unreachable error the spec promises (AC1.4/1.5/UX-flow 'error path' detail).
recommendation: Before calling response.json(), assert `response.ok` and throw `Error('Sui RPC ${method} returned HTTP ${response.status} from ${rpcUrl}. Verify the sandbox is running.')`. Wrap the response.json() call in try/catch and throw an analogous wrapping error for body-parse failures.

title: rpc() does not handle network-level fetch rejection (DNS, connection refused)
description: A `fetch(...)` call in the browser rejects with a `TypeError: Failed to fetch` (or in Node with `fetch failed` + cause `ECONNREFUSED`) when the host is unreachable, the port is closed, or DNS fails. `rpc()` does not wrap fetch in a try/catch, so the raw browser error message ('TypeError: Failed to fetch') propagates to App.useEffect and is shown to the user verbatim. That message names neither the RPC URL nor the sandbox boot recipe.
impact: The most common failure mode (sandbox not running, the prototypical RPC-unreachable case AC1.1 calls out) produces the least actionable error: an opaque browser TypeError rather than 'Sui RPC at http://127.0.0.1:9000 unreachable; run pnpm deploy-all from the deepbook-sandbox repo.' T-020 doesn't catch this because the test stubs fetchPoolStats with a pre-formatted message.
recommendation: Wrap the fetch call: `try { response = await fetch(...) } catch (err) { throw new Error(`Sui RPC at ${rpcUrl} unreachable (${(err as Error).message}). Run pnpm deploy-all from the deepbook-sandbox repo.`, { cause: err }); }`

title: rpc() casts result to T without checking the JSON-RPC envelope; missing `result` returns undefined
description: After parsing the JSON-RPC envelope, `rpc()` returns `env.result as T` without first checking that `env.result` exists. A well-formed JSON-RPC reply must have either `result` or `error`; an aberrant response (proxy injection, partial server impl) could have neither, in which case `rpc()` returns `undefined` typed as T and downstream code mis-types undefined as the expected shape. No explicit check; no log.
impact: Edge case — well-behaved Sui RPC servers won't trigger this — but a low-cost defensive check would prevent silent undefined propagation through `runDataLayer`'s `await rpc(...)` calls (which currently discard the result anyway, see R3-012).
recommendation: After the `if (env.error)` branch, add `if (env.result === undefined) throw new Error(`${method} returned no result and no error`);`

title: runDataLayer issues RPC calls but discards every result; failures-by-shape are invisible
description: `runDataLayer` loops over pools and `await`s `rpc(rpcUrl, 'sui_getObject', ...)` and `rpc(rpcUrl, 'suix_queryEvents', ...)`, then throws the responses on the floor (no assignment, no return value). The function's return type is `Promise<void>`. This is structurally fine for the T-014 network-shape test (which only spies on outbound URLs), but it means: (a) any unexpected response shape (e.g. queryEvents returning `{ data: undefined }`, or sui_getObject returning a non-pool object id) is silently ignored — `rpc` completes successfully, the result is discarded, and the for-loop moves on; (b) the function provides no path for the App to actually consume per-pool data; (c) it is a tautology relative to T-014 (the test passes because the function makes the right calls, but the function does nothing useful with the responses).
impact: Beyond the tautology concern (out-of-dimension), the error-handling consequence is that runDataLayer cannot surface any chain-shape mismatch. The two real-world failure modes T-020 and the spec's 'RPC returns unexpected shape' want covered are silent here: the only error class that propagates is the JSON-RPC `error` envelope or a fetch reject. A pool object that exists but lacks the expected `book` field would produce zero error signal.
recommendation: Either (a) make runDataLayer actually return per-pool data (and validate the response shape before returning), or (b) clearly mark it as an RPC-shape probe and add per-call shape assertions (e.g. `if (!result?.data?.content) throw ...`). The current shape provides false assurance — calls succeed, errors are impossible.

title: computeMarketStats calls BigInt(orderId) with no try/catch; invalid order_id throws SyntaxError
description: decodeAskPrice and decodeBidPrice both call `BigInt(orderId)` on `Order.order_id`, which is typed as `string` but ultimately sourced from chain JSON. If the chain ever returns a non-numeric string (sandbox-side bug, BCS deserialisation regression, or an order_id field renamed in a future DeepBook version), `BigInt(...)` throws a synchronous `SyntaxError: Cannot convert <x> to a BigInt`. computeMarketStats has no try/catch and propagates the throw to its caller, which in turn would (per R3-007) blank the entire dashboard. Similarly, `Number(o.quantity)` silently coerces non-numeric strings to NaN, and NaN levels then fail every `lvl.price >= lo && lvl.price <= hi` check (NaN comparisons are always false), so depth silently drops affected levels.
impact: The BigInt throw is a hard-crash path triggered by chain-shape drift — exactly what AC1.6 (chain-shape capture) was meant to defend against, but only at compile time. The NaN coercion silently miscounts depth without any signal. Both are low-probability today (the chain shape is captured), but T-007 explicitly demands graceful one-sided handling — graceful handling of malformed input is a peer concern.
recommendation: Wrap the order-id decode in try/catch and skip orders whose order_id fails to parse (with optional console.warn). Likewise, after `Number(o.quantity)`, guard with `Number.isFinite(qty)`; skip non-finite levels. Both changes preserve the happy-path numerics while preventing a single bad order from poisoning a whole pool's stats.

title: aggregateFills coerces fill price/quantity via Number() with no NaN guard
description: aggregateFills sums `Number(f.baseQuantity)` into `volume24h` and casts `Number(sorted[last].price)` for `lastPrice` without guarding against NaN. If a chain fill arrives with a malformed quantity or price string (chain-shape drift, missing field, BCS issue), the resulting NaN poisons the volume aggregate (NaN + N = NaN for the rest of the loop) and the lastPrice silently becomes NaN. PoolCard's `fmt` does guard against `!Number.isFinite(value)` and renders the sentinel, so the user gets '—' instead of a crash — but they get '—' for ALL fills in the day, not just the malformed one.
impact: Single bad fill record corrupts the whole day's volume. PoolCard sentinel masks the symptom — user sees '—' and assumes 'no trades' when the truth is 'one trade had a malformed quantity'. Low because the chain-shape capture is locked-in and field shapes are well-known, but this is a textbook silent-failure pattern: NaN propagation through aggregation.
recommendation: Guard each Number() call: `const q = Number(f.baseQuantity); if (Number.isFinite(q)) volume24h += q;` and similarly for price. Optional: count and surface a `malformedFills` integer in FillAggregate so the UI can show 'N/M trades unparseable'.

title: fetchFills loop has no upper bound on pagination; malformed RPC response could spin forever
description: fetchFills uses `while (true)` with three break conditions: 50 fills collected, window crossed, or `!response.hasNextPage`. There is no maximum-iteration safety bound. If a buggy or misbehaving queryEvents implementation returns `hasNextPage: true` indefinitely while always returning data older-than-24h-but-not-quite (so neither MAX_FILLS nor crossedWindow ever fires) or returns the SAME cursor each iteration, fetchFills loops forever and the App's per-pool fetch hangs (which Promise.all then waits on indefinitely — App stays in 'loading' status and never errors out).
impact: Hung loading state with no timeout. User sees 'Loading…' forever and has no signal that the data layer is stuck. Spec doesn't promise a fetch timeout, but the absence of any iteration cap turns 'misbehaving RPC' into 'infinite hang'.
recommendation: Add a hard iteration cap (e.g. `for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++)`) and throw an explicit 'queryEvents pagination exceeded N pages without satisfying stop conditions' error if the cap is reached. Alternatively detect cursor-no-advance (`if (newCursor === oldCursor) break-throw`).

title: fetchFills does not handle queryEvents returning non-array `data`
description: fetchFills assumes `response.data` is always an iterable array (`for (const ev of response.data)`). If the upstream queryEvents implementation ever returns `{ data: undefined, hasNextPage: false, nextCursor: null }` (which is a plausible JSON-RPC degraded-shape — and the dataLayer.rpc() helper would happily pass such a response through, see R3-011), the for...of loop throws `TypeError: response.data is not iterable`, which is then unhandled by fetchFills' caller (App.useEffect's try/catch will catch it, but the message will be the raw TypeError).
impact: Edge-case crash with a non-actionable error message. Unlikely in practice but a guard is one line.
recommendation: `if (!Array.isArray(response.data)) throw new Error('queryEvents returned non-array data field');` at the top of the loop body.

title: PoolCard fmt uses String(value) instead of toLocaleString/toFixed; fine numeric values render as 1.234e-7
description: Not strictly an error-handling defect, but adjacent: `fmt` returns `String(value)` for finite numbers, which produces JavaScript's default toString — including scientific notation for very small or very large values. The sparkline branch correctly uses `p.price.toFixed(4)`, but the six other fields don't. A genuine but tiny mid-price (e.g. 0.0000000123) would render as '1.23e-8', which a non-technical user might misread as the sentinel or as a broken value. This only matters because the data layer is currently stubbed to return zeros, so the issue is hidden — but it'll surface once R3-005 is fixed.
impact: Cosmetic now, latent UX bug after data layer is wired. Not load-bearing for any AC.
recommendation: Mirror the sparkline approach: `value.toLocaleString(undefined, { maximumFractionDigits: 6 })` or pin `toFixed(N)` per field per the stat's natural scale.
